open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51, where the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Note that Parrish et al.'s judges had 90 seconds of passage access, while Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage
Compare question sampling: Michael et al. keep only Gutenberg QuALITY-hard questions needing more than one or two sentences of context
out.other_title: Single-turn debate-style arguments do not improve human accuracy on hard QuALITY questions
out.rationale: Both studies ask whether debate helps human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension; Parrish et al. report a null result, while Michael et al. find debate beats consultancy (84% vs 74%). The authors say absolute accuracies are not comparable (p14 L47-48) and attribute the difference to protocol, so this challenges how far the null result generalizes, not its internal validity.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the contrast depends on protocol differences (length, judge interaction, expertise gap)

text: The authors note that in Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debate experiments on QuALITY, debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy, and they point to differences from their own setting. The first is that their debates have unbounded length, so debaters must keep defending their claims, which the authors suggest may produce more useful and informative arguments.
title: Michael et al. find debate helps QuALITY judges, unlike Parrish et al.'s single-turn null result
